newsitem.title: GERMANY: Welteke says German debate on EMU delay irrational.
newsitem.headline: Welteke says German debate on EMU delay irrational.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on Thursday that it was too late for Germany to start an irrational debate about the planned start of European monetary union, set for January 1, 1999.

Welteke told German television that the German public discussion on EMU was also focussing excessively on one particular criterion -- the requirement to cut budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
"One must acknowledge that....on the monetary targets -- prices, interest rates and currencies, developments have come so far that 14 of the 15 countries meet the goals," he said.

Asked to comment on the reasons why he held the view that the planned start of monetary union should not be delayed, Welteke said that discussions about the Treaty should have taken place years ago, when the agreement was ratified.
"We cannot behave as though we are at the start of a debate," he said.

"We agreed a Treaty of 15 countries... Many countries are taking the consequences and preparing for monetary union, while we are beginning a hectic debate about delay -- which is fuelled mostly by what I consider irrational arguments -- 20 months before the start," he added.

Welteke criticised German politicians for making one single criterion on deficits "an obsession, under which everyone is acting as though monetary union cannot begin under a particular deficit constellation."
But he added that budget reductions were necessary nonetheless.

"I would stress that it is necessary to consolidate the budget that has nothing to do with Maastricht or criteria...and that it wil be necessary for the individual members in monetary union to behave in a sound manner on fiscal issues, that is why the stability pact was discussed and agreed," he said.

Countries which wish to meld their currencies into the euro from 1999 must meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public debt and budget deficits this year in advance of a 1998 decision on which nations will take part.
Germany, in common with many other European nations, is facing serious problems in reaching the deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product.
Bonn's forecast for a deficit of 2.9 percent this year is deemed optimistic by many analysts.
